title: How Steve Jobs framed the Macintosh as the "telephone" of computing and rallied Apple against IBM
summary: Jobs argues that technology only wins when ordinary people can use it without learning "strange incantations," comparing the telegraph and telephone to the IBM PC and Macintosh. He says Macintosh lets people express themselves and injects a liberal-arts spirit into business. His 1983 sales-meeting speech casts Apple as the last obstacle to IBM control and introduces the "1984" ad.

principles.text: Technology that demands arcane commands will not reach most people; it has to be something they already know how to use.
principles.quote: Most people are not going to learn slash-qz’s any more than they’re going to learn Morse code.

principles.text: Great products let people express themselves, not just complete a function.
principles.quote: Macintosh lets you sing. It lets you use special fonts. It lets you make drawings and pictures or incorporate other people’s drawings or pictures into your documents.

principles.text: Better visual communication cuts clutter and raises the quality of communication.
principles.quote: Even in business, you’re seeing five-page memos get compressed down to a one-page memo because there’s a picture to express the key concept.

principles.text: Work tools should be fun; inject the liberal-arts spirit into serious business.
principles.quote: if we can again inject that liberal-arts spirit into this very serious realm of business, I think it would be a worthwhile contribution.

principles.text: Incumbents dismiss new categories as too small to matter, and miss them; use that history to rally your team against the dominant player.
principles.quote: IBM dismisses the personal computer as too small to do serious computing and unimportant to their business.
